clue.text: New visa helps to reach this illegal vessel of LeRoi Jones

definitions.note: LeRoi Jones (Amiri Baraka) wrote the play Slave Ship, about a vessel in the outlawed trade

indicators.note: something new is freshly made, so the letters of the two words are made over in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A fresh visa helps someone reach a smuggling boat from a play by LeRoi Jones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' signals an anagram of VISA HELPS; 'to reach this' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The slave trade's carriers were outlawed ships, and Slave Ship is the title of a 1967 play by LeRoi Jones.

clue.text: Reading matter literally outlandish

parts.note: books and objects from far-off places, things that are foreign and strange, read as a kind of literature

explanation.surface: Some books are, quite literally, out of this world.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means curious things from foreign lands, outlandish by origin, and is used for collections of strange writings.

clue.text: Cold fool and artist becomes soothsayer

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
an ass is a foolish person
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A chilly idiot who paints turns into a prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becomes' is a link. RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's usual artist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the Trojan princess was a prophet fated never to be believed, so her name stands for any seer of doom.

clue.text: He offered us a good night out

definitions.text: He offered us a good night out

parts.words: He offered us a good night out
parts.note: a Scottish playwright whose book on popular theatre was titled A Good Night Out

explanation.surface: Someone treated us to an enjoyable evening.
explanation.walkthrough: John McGrath, founder of the 7:84 theatre company, wrote A Good Night Out about theatre for working-class audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright John McGrath literally offered readers A Good Night Out, the title of his lectures on popular theatre.

clue.text: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia

definitions.text: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia

parts.words: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia
parts.note: in Fielding's Tom Jones the heroine Sophia's aunt boasts of having turned down titled suitors

explanation.surface: A proud lady's niece reports that she turned down a noble offer of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: In Fielding's Tom Jones, Squire Western's sister, Sophia's aunt, prides herself on having rejected offers from titled men.

clue.text: Loyalist opposed to Cade is off, for example, in a disturbed state

indicators.note: letters that are disturbed are shaken out of order, so these get rearranged

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A king's man fighting the rebel Jack Cade is off his head with worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link. In Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2, Matthew Goffe is the royal officer killed resisting Jack Cade's rebels in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Goffe fought for the king against Jack Cade's rebellion, a loyal soldier in Shakespeare's history play.

clue.text: It is the Ordinary made beautiful; it is also the —— made lethal" (Peter Shaffer, Equus)

definitions.text: It is the Ordinary made beautiful; it is also the —— made lethal" (Peter Shaffer, Equus)

parts.words: It is the Ordinary made beautiful; it is also the —— made lethal" (Peter Shaffer, Equus)
parts.note: Dysart's speech in Equus on the Normal: a missing word for the commonplace or mean, opposite the Ordinary

explanation.surface: A quotation from Peter Shaffer's play Equus with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The psychiatrist Dysart says of the Normal that it is the Ordinary made beautiful and the Average made lethal.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a word for the typical or mean, a near-synonym of ordinary, as in Shaffer's line.

clue.text: Heads turned for brother of Zeus

indicators.note: turned over, the letters of the word are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: Heads turned when the brother of Zeus appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the god of the underworld was a son of Cronus and so a brother of Zeus and Poseidon.

clue.text: Write-off for Inge's bloomers

parts.note: a dead loss, and the opening of William Inge's play title A ___ of Roses, roses being the bloomers

explanation.surface: Someone's embarrassing knickers are a complete write-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' suggests underwear, but it means flowers: William Inge, the American playwright, wrote A Loss of Roses.
explanation.definitionFit: A write-off is something counted as lost, and Inge's play is A Loss of Roses.

clue.text: Poet makes same arrangements with foxhunters

indicators.note: arrangements put things in a new order, so the letters of the preceding word are rearranged

parts.note: the field is the body of riders following a hunt

explanation.surface: A poet arranges the same thing with the local hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' and 'with' are links: 'arrangements' gives MASE from SAME. The poet laureate John Masefield wrote Reynard the Fox, about a hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: John Masefield was Poet Laureate from 1930 to 1967.

clue.text: Point to type size, large or on a large scale

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass
pica is a size of type, twelve points
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A printer points to a type size for big lettering.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic works are grand in scale, and the adjective describes things on that heroic, sweeping scale.

clue.text: Spartan king whose wife's looks may have created activity at boatyard

definitions.text: Spartan king whose wife's looks may have created activity at boatyard

parts.words: Spartan king whose wife's looks may have created activity at boatyard
parts.note: Helen's was the face that launched a thousand ships, so her beauty kept shipwrights busy; her husband ruled Sparta

explanation.surface: A Greek ruler's wife was so beautiful that the shipyards got busy.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen of Troy was the wife of the King of Sparta, and Marlowe called hers the face that launched a thousand ships.

clue.text: Guide on the river in David Copperfield

definitions.text: Guide on the river in David Copperfield

parts.note: to steer is to guide a course
the Forth is a Scottish river flowing into the Firth of Forth

explanation.surface: Someone piloting a boat on a river appears in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sets one piece after the other. James Steerforth, David's charming friend in David Copperfield, drowns in a storm at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Steerforth is David's charismatic school friend in Dickens's novel, who seduces Little Em'ly.

clue.text: Cousin to Kingsley's Salvation taken in by audience

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Cousin to Kingsley's Salvation taken in by audience (5)': 'taken in by audience' gives the answer, but no source found links the answer to Salvation Yeo of Kingsley's Westward Ho!, so the first definition cannot be explained

clue.text: Act on name of book indicating the owner

parts.note: a book's name is its title
a deed is an act or action

explanation.surface: Someone takes action on a book's title, showing who owns it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places Act's synonym after the other piece in the across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: This legal document proves who holds a property, the paper that names its proprietor.

clue.text: Poet's strange device

parts.note: Longfellow's youth bears 'a banner with the strange device', the Latin motto that is the poem's title

explanation.surface: A poet has invented an odd gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'device' suggests a gadget; in heraldry it is a motto on a banner, as in Longfellow's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: In Longfellow's poem the motto on the banner, meaning ever higher, is called a strange device.

clue.text: Churchyard offered one of rebellion

parts.note: Thomas Churchyard, Elizabethan poet

explanation.surface: A graveyard hosted an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Churchyard' looks like a burial ground but is the Elizabethan writer Thomas Churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Churchyard's 1570 pamphlet was a treatise, or extended talk, titled A Discourse of Rebellion.

clue.text: Marryat featured her man

parts.note: Captain Marryat's novel The ...: the title is this word plus 's man'

explanation.surface: A novelist wrote about a woman's husband.
explanation.walkthrough: Frederick Marryat, naval officer and novelist, wrote The Privateersman (1846); 'her man' plays on the title's ending.
explanation.definitionFit: A privately owned armed ship licensed to raid enemy shipping, whose crewman is Marryat's title character.

clue.text: Seen as metaphor by Sontag

parts.note: Susan Sontag's 1978 essay on how diseases such as cancer and TB are described in figurative terms

explanation.surface: Susan Sontag treated something as a figure of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan Sontag's essay Illness as Metaphor examines how sickness is turned into symbol.

clue.text: Writer whose name was made from putting heads together

definitions.text: Writer whose name was made from putting heads together

parts.words: Writer whose name was made from putting heads together
parts.note: headlands are also called by this word, so a collection of heads gives the surname of the writer Bernard ...

explanation.surface: An author got his name through collaborative brainstorming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting heads together' suggests conferring; here heads are headlands, and several of them make the plural surname of the Victorian writer Bernard Capes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is a headland, so heads together make the surname of Bernard Capes, author of ghost stories.

clue.text: Net play rewritten as set piece

indicators.note: something rewritten is put together again differently, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A tennis rally at the net is redrafted as a staged scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link. 'Net play' and 'set piece' suggest tennis or theatre; the answer is football.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a spot kick is a set piece, a planned restart from a dead ball.

clue.text: Vaughan Williams portrayed him in love

definitions.text: Vaughan Williams portrayed him in love

parts.words: Vaughan Williams portrayed him in love
parts.note: Vaughan Williams's opera Sir John in Love is based on The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: A composer depicted a man smitten with romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fat knight, Sir John, is the lovesick hero of Vaughan Williams's opera Sir John in Love.

clue.text: Destined to be free, wrote Jean Ingelow

definitions.text: Destined to be free, wrote Jean Ingelow

parts.words: Destined to be free, wrote Jean Ingelow
parts.note: the Victorian poet and novelist Jean Ingelow wrote the novel ... to be Free (1875)

explanation.surface: A poet declared that liberty was someone's destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Destined and this word are synonyms, and Ingelow's novel is titled Fated to be Free.

clue.text: Composer from Quito sticks to light music

indicators.note: the composer's name is taken out from within the run of letters in these two words

explanation.surface: A composer from Ecuador's capital keeps to lighter music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to light music' adds colour: Paolo Tosti wrote popular parlour songs.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesco Paolo Tosti was an Italian composer of salon songs such as Goodbye.

clue.text: Home entertainment seen as tragedy

parts.note: John Home, Scottish dramatist of Douglas

explanation.surface: Watching TV at home is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home entertainment' suggests TV; Home is the dramatist John Home, whose tragedy Alonzo was staged in 1773.
explanation.definitionFit: Alonzo is the title of John Home's 1773 tragedy, a play by Home.

clue.text: Like it may be in Wilson's book (through sorcery)

definitions.text: Like it may be in Wilson's book (through sorcery)

parts.words: Like it may be in Wilson's book (through sorcery)
parts.note: The title's opening, completed by 'by magic' (through sorcery)

explanation.surface: Things in a Wilson novel seem to happen by witchcraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'in the way it might be', and Angus Wilson's novel is As If by Magic.

clue.text: Those of time unearthed in lively account

definitions.text: Those of time unearthed in lively account

parts.words: Those of time unearthed in lively account
parts.note: Penelope Lively's 1979 novel ... of Time concerns an archaeologist's discoveries

explanation.surface: Relics of the past are dug up in a vivid narrative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lively' looks like an adjective but is the novelist Penelope Lively.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasures of Time is Penelope Lively's novel about an archaeologist; such valuables are dug up.

clue.text: Johnson's essays less industrious

definitions.meaning: Samuel Johnson's weekly essay series of 1758 to 1760 ran under this title

explanation.surface: Samuel Johnson's essays were not his most hard-working output.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's essays appeared as The Idler, and an idler is lazier than a worker.

clue.text: Couplet from parodist I cherished

indicators.note: the definition's word is picked out of the letters running across these clue words

explanation.surface: A treasured couplet comes from a parodist.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody a pair of verse lines forming a unit is a distich.
